title: Macrocytic Anaemia
subject: Medicine
summary: Macrocytic anaemia is defined by an MCV >100 fL and includes megaloblastic and non‑megaloblastic causes. In low‑resource settings, vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies, alcohol, and certain infections are common.

sections.p: A haemoglobin concentration below the age‑ and sex‑adjusted normal with a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) greater than 100 fL defines macrocytic anaemia. Peripheral smear shows macro‑ovalocytes; hypersegmented neutrophils suggest a megaloblastic aetiology.
b: MCV >100 fL
Macro‑ovalocytes on smear
Hypersegmented neutrophils → megaloblastic

sections.p: Severity is graded by haemoglobin: mild (10–12 g/dL), moderate (8–9.9 g/dL), severe (<8 g/dL). Staging guides urgency of transfusion and need for inpatient care.
b: Mild 10–12 g/dL
Moderate 8–9.9 g/dL
Severe <8 g/dL

sections.p: In East African and other low‑resource hospitals the commonest causes are nutritional deficiencies, alcohol, and infections that impair absorption or increase demand.
b: Vitamin B12 deficiency – pernicious anaemia, fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum), malabsorption (HIV, TB enteritis)
Folate deficiency – poor diet, chronic alcoholism, antiepileptic drugs
Alcohol excess – direct marrow toxicity, folate loss
Drugs interfering with DNA synthesis – methotrexate, zidovudine, chloramphenicol
Bone‑marrow failure – myelodysplastic syndromes, aplastic anaemia
Hemolysis with reticulocytosis – sickle cell crisis, malaria

sections.p: Patients present with fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, tachycardia and pallor. B12 deficiency adds peripheral neuropathy (paresthesiae, loss of vibration, extensor plantar response) and cognitive change.
b: Fatigue, dyspnoea, tachycardia
Pallor, glossitis
Neuropathy, dorsal column signs in B12 deficiency

t.b: Confirms macrocytosis and severity of anaemia
Low B12 confirms deficiency; if unavailable, treat empirically when clinical picture fits
Low folate points to folate deficiency; useful when B12 is normal
Elevated retics suggest haemolysis or marrow recovery; low retics indicate production problem
Distinguishes pernicious anaemia (corrected with intrinsic factor) from malabsorption
Identify infections causing malabsorption or marrow suppression

sections.p: Unrecognised B12 deficiency can lead to irreversible subacute combined degeneration. Severe anaemia (<8 g/dL) risks cardiac failure. Untreated folate deficiency in pregnancy causes neural‑tube defects.
b: Neurological deterioration
Heart failure from severe anaemia
Neural‑tube defects in pregnancy

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive therapy. Vitamin replacement must precede carbohydrate loads to avoid precipitating neuro‑injury.
b: Alcohol‑related – abstinence, folate supplementation, nutritional rehab
Drug‑induced – stop offending drug, consider alternative therapy
Severe anaemia – transfuse packed RBCs if symptomatic or Hb <7 g/dL

sections.p: Re‑check haemoglobin and MCV after 4–6 weeks of therapy. In endemic areas, screen high‑risk groups (vegetarians, HIV patients) and provide dietary education.
b: Repeat CBC and B12/folate after treatment
Educate on fortified foods, animal‑source protein
Treat helminth infections (Diphyllobothrium) with praziquantel

sections.p: Macrocytic anaemia can be mistaken for normocytic anaemia with high MCV due to reticulocytosis, or for sideroblastic anaemia which shows dimorphic cells.
b: Reticulocytosis – high MCV but normal B12/folate
Sideroblastic anaemia – ringed sideroblasts, iron overload

sections.p: Serum B12 may be normal in early deficiency; functional tests (methylmalonic acid) are unavailable in many settings. Folate levels can be falsely low after recent meals.
b: Normal B12 with neurological signs → consider functional deficiency
Low folate after alcohol binge → transient

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of limb sensation or gait instability
Chest pain or severe dyspnoea with anaemia

faq.a: Folate can correct the anaemia but does not treat the neurological damage of B12 deficiency, so B12 must be replaced first.
Severe malaria can cause reticulocytosis, raising MCV, but true macrocytic anaemia is usually due to nutritional or drug causes.
Yes, it helps differentiate megaloblastic from non‑megaloblastic causes and detects hypersegmented neutrophils.

exam: A 32‑year‑old HIV‑positive woman presents with fatigue, glossitis and MCV 112 fL. What is your next diagnostic step — order serum B12 and folate, because deficiency is most likely in this setting.
A patient with known alcohol dependence has MCV 108 fL but normal B12 and folate. Which cause should you consider first — alcohol‑related folate loss and direct marrow toxicity.
You see a patient with macrocytic anaemia and a positive Schilling test after intrinsic factor. What does this indicate — pernicious anaemia; treat with lifelong B12 injections.
A child from a rural area has macrocytosis, abdominal pain and recent fish consumption. Which infection is relevant — Diphyllobothrium latum tapeworm causing B12 deficiency.

During a ward round you encounter severe macrocytic anaemia (Hb 6.5 g/dL) with tachycardia. What immediate management is required — give oxygen, monitor vitals and arrange urgent packed RBC transfusion.
Explain why giving high‑dose folic acid alone to a B12‑deficient patient can be dangerous — it may correct the anaemia while neurological injury progresses, leading to irreversible damage.
A patient on zidovudine develops macrocytosis. How should you modify therapy — assess need for the drug, consider dose reduction or switch, and supplement folate if needed.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent neuro‑imaging in a macrocytic anaemia patient — new onset gait ataxia or progressive weakness suggesting spinal cord involvement.
